summary: Describes the timing issues in rolling a key in a DNSSEC-signed zone. It presents timelines and shows how parameters such as TTLs and signature lifetimes interact, so operators can change keys without breaking validation.

plainLanguage.summary: Changing the lock on a door must be timed so nobody is locked out while old keys still circulate.

questions: how long should a dnssec rollover take
what is a dnssec key rollover
subtitle: How to time the replacement of DNSSEC keys so no part of a signed zone ever fails validation.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC keys, signatures and DS records are cached by resolvers, so swapping a key carelessly can make a zone fail validation for some clients.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out step-by-step timelines for rolling Zone Signing Keys and Key Signing Keys, with formulas built from propagation delays and TTLs that say when each step is safe.
tldr.outcome: It recommends Pre-Publication for ZSKs and calls Double-RRset the most efficient KSK method, and it advises standby keys for emergencies.

today: RFC 7583 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes current thinking at the time of publication in October 2015 and says the subject matter is evolving.

sections.title: Why Key Timing Matters
sections.content:
A zone manager must be ready to replace (roll) the keys used to sign a DNSSEC zone, whether after a compromise or because policy demands periodic replacement. DNSKEY records, DS records and RRSIG records are held by authoritative servers and also cached by resolvers, so a validating resolver may combine a cached signature with a separately fetched key.

The goal of key management logic is not to finish a rollover at a set time but to make no change until it is safe, meaning that no part of the zone ever goes bogus. A ZSK authenticates data within the zone, and its signature and key come from the same zone. A KSK authenticates the DNSKEY RRset, and its DS record comes from the parent zone. The document does not cover keys used as both ZSK and KSK, algorithm rollovers, or changing TTLs.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people keep copies of old notes. Before you swap a key you have to wait until all those old notes are gone, or someone will be confused.

sections.title: Rollover Methods and Key States
sections.content:
A ZSK can be rolled three ways. Pre-Publication adds the new key, waits for caches, then switches signatures and later removes the old key. Double-Signature adds the new key and signatures while keeping the old ones, the simplest and fastest but it enlarges the zone and responses. Double-RRSIG adds new signatures without a new key, and the RFC says it is unlikely to be used and does not consider it further.

A KSK can also be rolled three ways: Double-KSK (new key first, then the DS record, then remove the old key), Double-DS (new DS first, then the key, then remove the old DS) and Double-RRset (new key and new DS together, then remove both old ones).

Keys move through the states Generated, Published, Ready, Active, Retired, Dead and Removed. A Revoked state is used when RFC 5011 trust anchor handling applies.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add the new key before taking away the old one, or the other way around. Each way trades speed against how much extra stuff you carry for a while.

sections.title: ZSK Rollover Timelines
sections.content:
In Pre-Publication, key N is published, and after the publication interval Ipub = Dprp + TTLkey it is ready. Here Dprp is the propagation delay to all nameservers and TTLkey the DNSKEY TTL. Later it becomes active and signs RRsets. Its successor must be published at least Ipub before it is needed. When the lifetime Lzsk ends, key N is retired and key N+1 activated.

The retired key stays for the retire interval Iret = Dsgn + Dprp + TTLsig, where Dsgn is the time to re-sign everything and TTLsig the maximum RRSIG TTL. After the dead time it can be removed.

In Double-Signature, the retire interval is Iret = Dsgn + Dprp + max(TTLkey, TTLsig), and the old key and signatures are removed only after that.
sections.plainLanguage: You show everyone the new key first, wait long enough that all of them have seen it, then start using it, then wait again before throwing out the old one.

sections.title: KSK Rollover Timelines
sections.content:
KSK timing involves the parent zone, so the zone manager does not control it all. A delay called Dreg, the registration delay, covers the time between submitting a DS record to the parent and its appearance there. If the parent is slow, the effect is only a slowdown in the rollover, not an operational problem.

In Double-KSK, the new key is published and becomes ready after IpubC = DprpC + TTLkey. The DS record is then submitted, and the key is active at Tact = Tsbm + Dreg. The old key is kept for Iret = DprpP + TTLds after the DS record is replaced. Double-DS reverses the order, with the DS publication interval IpubP = DprpP + TTLds.

If a key is also configured as a trust anchor, RFC 5011 timings apply, including a revoke step. For the first keys of a zone there are no timing rules, except the DS record must not appear in a secure parent before the DNSKEY can be obtained.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the main key means asking the parent zone to update its records too. That takes time you cannot control, so you wait until they confirm.

sections.title: Standby Keys and Algorithms
sections.content:
For an emergency rollover, a key must be in the ready state before it can sign, so keeping at least one extra standby key ready minimizes delay. For ZSKs a standby key only makes sense with Pre-Publication. A standby KSK should also sign the DNSKEY RRset, otherwise waiting for the old RRset to expire erases the time saving. With Double-DS, the standby item is a DS record in the parent.

Each algorithm in the zone can be rolled independently, because the rollover logic is run separately per algorithm. The RFC recommends Pre-Publication for ZSKs, and Double-RRset as the most efficient KSK method. Standby keys should be standard practice. Security considerations add no new issues beyond RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035 and RFC 5011.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep a spare key ready in the drawer so that if the lock is ever broken you can swap right away.

cells: New key, then DS change, then remove old key
Few parent interactions; larger DNSKEY RRset
New DS, then key change, then remove old DS

New key and DS together, then remove old
Fastest; larger RRset and two parent interactions
